traveler: Alexander the Great (Alexandros III of Macedon)
title: Pella to Babylon: the Son of Ammon and the Ends of the Earth
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Pella and the Making of a King

stops.name: Pella, the birth of the king
stops.campa: In the palace at Pella, Olympias bears a son to Philip on the sixth of Hecatombaeon, and the omens crowd in at once: she had dreamed, the night before her marriage, that a thunderbolt struck her womb and kindled a fire that spread far and went out; Philip had dreamed he sealed her body with the image of a lion. On this same night, far off at Ephesus, the Temple of Artemis burns to the ground, fired by a madman named Herostratus. The seers say the goddess was too busy attending this birth to save her own house.
suggested_refs: The ruins of the royal palace at Pella, Alexander's birthplace
The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, burned the night of his birth

stops.name: Pella, the taming of Bucephalus
stops.campa: Philoneicus the Thessalian offers Philip a black stallion for thirteen talents, but the horse rears and will let no man mount him, and the king orders it led away. The boy Alexander, watching, cries out what a horse they are losing for want of skill to handle him, and wagers the price of the animal that he can ride it. He has seen what the grooms missed: the horse shies from its own shadow. He turns its head to the sun, strokes it, springs up, and gallops him. Philip weeps and kisses his son.
stops.quote: What a horse they are losing, because, for lack of skill and courage, they cannot manage him!
suggested_refs: Bucephalus, Alexander's warhorse, ridden until India
Philip's saying to his son: 'seek a kingdom equal to and worthy of thyself, for Macedonia is too little for thee'

stops.name: Mieza, the garden of Aristotle
stops.campa: Philip brings Aristotle from Stagira and sets him over Alexander's schooling in the quiet nymph-haunted grove of Mieza, among the Nymphaeum's caves and colonnades, its stone benches and shaded walks. Here for some years the two talk through ethics, politics, medicine, the structure of plants and beasts, and above all Homer: Aristotle edits a copy of the Iliad for his pupil, who will keep it always under his pillow with his dagger, calling it his viaticum of the art of war. When Aristotle later publishes these lectures, Alexander writes to reproach him: what will set him above other men now?
stops.quote: Thou hast not done well to publish thy acroamatic doctrines; for in what shall I surpass other men if those doctrines wherein I have been trained are to be all men's common property?
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 7 (Perrin), Alexander's letter to Aristotle
suggested_refs: The Nymphaeum of Mieza, the caves and colonnade of Aristotle's school
Alexander's annotated 'casket copy' of the Iliad, carried on campaign

stops.name: Chaeronea, the Sacred Band destroyed
stops.campa: Eighteen years old, Alexander is given command of the Companion cavalry on the left wing while Philip holds the right. When the Theban line at last opens a gap by the riverbank, Alexander drives his horse through it before any order is given, and the Sacred Band of Thebes, three hundred sworn lovers and friends who have never before broken rank, is surrounded and cut down where it stands, refusing to yield ground even in death. The battle breaks the free cities of Greece; Philip weeps over the fallen Thebans and lets his son's charge be called the day's turn.
suggested_refs: The Lion of Chaeronea, raised over the mass grave of the Sacred Band

stops.name: Aegae, the murder of Philip and the throne
stops.campa: In the theater at Aegae, amid the wedding festival of his daughter, Philip walks in procession between two Alexanders, his son and his son-in-law, dressed plainly to show the crowd he needs no bodyguard. His own guardsman Pausanias, nursing an old unavenged wrong, runs forward and drives a dagger between his ribs; fleeing to a waiting horse, Pausanias trips on a vine-root and is cut down by the king's companions before he can be questioned. Within the hour the army and the nobles of Macedon proclaim the twenty-year-old Alexander king in his father's blood-soaked place.
suggested_refs: The royal tombs at Aegae/Vergina, Philip II's burial place
The theater of Aegae, site of the assassination

stops.name: Corinth, the League and Diogenes
stops.campa: The Greek states, assembled at the Isthmus, confirm the new king as hegemon of the League his father built and general of the war against Persia, as they once named Philip. While at Corinth, Alexander seeks out Diogenes the Cynic, who lives in a storage jar and owns nothing, and finds him sunning himself. Offered whatever he wishes, Diogenes asks only that the king stop blocking his sun. Alexander's companions mock the beggar-philosopher on the road home; Alexander silences them, saying that were he not himself, this is the only other man he would choose to be.
stops.quote: But verily, if I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.
suggested_refs: Diogenes' pithos (storage-jar) at the Craneum of Corinth
The League of Corinth's decree naming Alexander hegemon
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers 6.38

stops.name: The Danube, the crossing against the Getae
stops.campa: Before he can turn to Asia, Alexander must secure his back: he storms the Shipka Pass, breaks the Triballi, and comes to the Ister, the greatest river of Europe. His warships cannot force the current, so by night his men stuff their leather tents with hay and ferry four thousand foot and fifteen hundred horse across through standing corn that hides them until dawn. The Getae army of fourteen thousand, astonished that this river has been crossed at all, breaks and flees at the first charge, abandoning their town to a king barely turned twenty-one.
suggested_refs: Arrian's account of the Danube crossing, Anabasis of Alexander Book 1

stops.name: Thebes destroyed, the house of Pindar spared
stops.campa: Word reaches the Balkan camp that Thebes, told falsely that Alexander has died fighting the Illyrians, has revolted and besieged the Macedonian garrison. He force-marches south in thirteen days and offers terms; the Thebans refuse and are stormed. Six thousand die and thirty thousand are sold into slavery, the city razed stone from stone, on the vote of the allied Greeks who hated it of old. Alexander orders one house spared among the ruin, and posts the order over its door himself, for the sake of the poet who lived there a hundred and thirty years before.
suggested_refs: The house of Pindar at Thebes, the sole dwelling left standing
The Cadmea, the citadel of Thebes, garrisoned afterward

stops.name: The Hellespont, the spear cast into Asia
stops.campa: From Elaeus, Alexander steers the flagship himself across the strait, and at midchannel slaughters a bull to Poseidon and pours a libation from a golden bowl to the Nereids, asking safe crossing for the army of forty thousand behind him. Nearing the Asian shore he arms himself fully in the bow. As the hull grinds onto the sand he hurls his spear ahead of him into the soil of the Persian empire and leaps down among the first men ashore, claiming the whole continent, by the spear and by the gift of the gods, before a single battle is fought.
suggested_refs: The Dardanelles (Hellespont) crossing point near Abydos and Sestos

stops.name: Troy, the tomb of Achilles and the shield of the gods
stops.campa: At Ilium, Alexander climbs to the citadel and sacrifices to Trojan Athena, dedicating his own armor and taking down in exchange arms said to have hung there since the Trojan War, which his shield-bearers will carry before him into every battle after. He anoints the pillar over Achilles' tomb with oil and runs the traditional race naked around it with his companions, crowning it with a wreath, while Hephaestion does the same at the grave of Patroclus. Alexander, who claims Achilles as his mother's ancestor, calls him blessed to have found, in life, a friend, and after death, a Homer.
stops.quote: O fortunate youth, who have found in Homer a herald of your valour!
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Pro Archia 10.24 ('o fortunate adulescens, qui tuae virtutis Homerum praeconem inveneris!'), spoken at Achilles' tomb at Sigeum; cf. Plutarch, Life of Alexander 15
suggested_refs: The tumulus traditionally named the Tomb of Achilles near Troy
The 'sacred shield' from the Temple of Athena at Ilium, carried before Alexander in battle

stops.name: Granicus, the first battle and the cracked helmet
stops.campa: The Persian satraps line the far bank of the Granicus, expecting the river itself to break the Macedonian charge. Alexander leads the Companions straight into the current and the steep bank beyond. In the melee the Persian Rhoesaces splits his helmet and shears away its plume with a stroke that would have opened his skull; Alexander runs him through, but Spithridates is already swinging from behind when Cleitus, called the Black, severs the arm at the shoulder and saves the king's life. The Persian line breaks; the Greek mercenaries in Persian pay are surrounded and slaughtered almost to a man.
suggested_refs: The 300 Persian panoplies Alexander sent to Athens after Granicus, inscribed to all Greeks save the Spartans

segments.name: Gordium to Gaza: the Coastal Kingdom

stops.name: Gordium, the knot cut
stops.campa: In the old Phrygian citadel stands the wagon of Gordius, its yoke lashed to the pole by a knot of cornel bark with no visible end, which oracle says will be undone only by the man fated to rule all Asia. Alexander, unable to find the ends by working the cords, will not be seen to fail before the watching army: he sets his sword to the tangle and cuts it through with one stroke, or, as Aristobulus tells it, simply draws out the pin that holds the pole and slips the yoke free. Either way, that night lightning and thunder confirm the sign.
stops.quote: It makes no difference how they are loosed.
stops.quote_source: Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 3.1.18 ('nihil, inquit, interest quomodo solvantur'); Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.3 gives the linchpin version, after Aristobulus
suggested_refs: The Gordian Knot, cut at the citadel of ancient Gordium (Yassıhöyük)

stops.name: Issus, the Great King in flight and the captured queen mother
stops.campa: Darius, cutting behind Alexander onto this narrow coastal plain, is broken when Alexander drives his companions straight at the Persian center; Darius abandons shield, bow, and royal cloak to escape on a fresher horse, leaving his mother, wife, and children behind in the captured camp. Alexander and Hephaestion go to promise the women safety; the old queen Sisygambis, mistaking the taller Hephaestion for the king, bows to him first and is covered in shame at her error. Alexander raises her, saying she has not erred, for Hephaestion too is an Alexander, and claims Darius's own tent that night, remarking that this, it seems, is what it is to be a king.
stops.quote: You did not err, mother; for he too is Alexander.
stops.quote_source: Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 3.12.17 ('non errasti, mater; nam et hic Alexander est'); Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.37
suggested_refs: The Alexander Mosaic of Pompeii, depicting the charge at Issus
Charles Le Brun's 'The Tent of Darius' (1661), depicting the Sisygambis scene

stops.name: Tyre, the dream of the god and the causeway
stops.campa: Tyre, an island fortress with walls rising straight from the sea, refuses Alexander entry even to sacrifice to its god Melqart, whom the Greeks call Heracles and count among Alexander's own ancestors. He answers with a mole of stone, timber, and rubble driven straight across the strait toward the walls, under constant fire from the towers and fire-ships of the Tyrians. In the city, the high priest dreams that Melqart is leaving Tyre to walk beside Alexander's camp; in Alexander's own camp, the seer Aristander reads a satyr dancing on his shield as a Greek pun: sa Tyros, Tyre is yours.
suggested_refs: The submerged remains of Alexander's mole, now the isthmus joining Tyre to the mainland
The Temple of Melqart-Heracles at Tyre

stops.name: Tyre, the king descends in a vessel of glass
stops.campa: To see with his own eyes what the Tyrians have built beneath the waves against his causeway, Alexander has a great barrel of clear glass made, sealed and chained, and has himself lowered into the harbor depths. Around him move the shapes of the deep, vast and voracious, feeding without pity on the small and the weak, and the king watches in silence a long while before signaling to be drawn up. When he stands again on his own deck he tells his officers plainly what he has learned of the world below the world, and it unsettles them more than any siege.
stops.quote: The world is damned and lost: the great and powerful fish devour the small fry.
stops.quote_source: The Alexander Romance, glass-vessel descent (Pseudo-Callisthenes and its vernacular daughters); the moral of the great fish devouring the small is the medieval Western retelling's, not the Greek recension's
suggested_refs: Medieval manuscript illuminations of Alexander's glass diving-bell (e.g. the Talbot Shrewsbury Book, 15th c.)
sources: Alexander Romance, Pseudo-Callisthenes recension gamma / the diving-bell legend

stops.name: Gaza, the wound and the dust of Achilles
stops.campa: Batis, eunuch commander of Gaza, holds the last fortress before Egypt and answers Alexander's summons with silent defiance, trusting his high mound and his tunnels dug under the siege-works. Three assaults fail; in the second, a bolt from a catapult drives through Alexander's shield and breastplate into his shoulder, and he fights on wounded. When the walls fall at last after two months, Batis is taken alive, and Alexander, remembering Achilles dragging Hector behind his chariot beneath the walls of Troy, has a cord run through Batis's heels and drags him living around the city until he dies.
suggested_refs: Quintus Curtius Rufus's account of the death of Batis, read against Iliad 22

segments.name: Egypt and the Son of Ammon

stops.name: Memphis, the crowning of the pharaoh
stops.campa: Egypt, chafing two centuries under Persian tax and Persian gods, opens its gates without a blow; the satrap Mazaces surrenders Pelusium and Memphis both, and the crowds hail Alexander as liberator. In Memphis he sacrifices to Apis, the sacred bull the Persians had mocked and, some say, killed, and the priests of Ptah anoint him upon the ancient throne with the double crown, naming him Son of Ra and Beloved of Amun in the unbroken formula they have given every pharaoh for three thousand years. He holds games there, Greek athletes and poets performing before the oldest kingship on earth.
suggested_refs: Alexander's hieroglyphic cartouche as Pharaoh of Egypt, carved at Karnak and Luxor

stops.name: Alexandria, the city outlined in barley and devoured by birds
stops.campa: Between the sea and Lake Mareotis, Alexander walks the ground himself and marks out the streets, the agora, the sanctuaries of a city to bear his name, in the shape of a soldier's cloak. Having no chalk, the engineers pour out the army's barley meal along his lines; before the walls can even be surveyed, birds descend on the outline from the river and the marsh in uncounted thousands and eat every grain. The seers, watching Alexander's face darken, tell him the sign is good beyond reading: the city will feed multitudes from every nation and never want for bread.
suggested_refs: Alexandria, Egypt, founded on this plan and still bearing his name
The lost Lighthouse (Pharos) and Library, built by his successors on this ground

stops.name: Siwa, the oracle names the son of god
stops.campa: Across days of waterless desert and blinding wind, twice saved, the tradition says, by ravens or serpents sent to guide the lost column and by a sudden storm of rain, Alexander reaches the green spring-fed oasis and the oracle-shrine of Ammon, whom the Greeks read as Zeus. The priest, they say confused by his own Greek, greets him not as Ammon's servant but as his son. Inside the sanctuary alone, Alexander asks his questions and hears his answers; he tells his companions afterward only that he has heard what was agreeable to his wishes, and never repeats the rest to any man alive.
stops.quote: I have heard what was agreeable to my wishes.
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.4 (reported as Alexander's own account of the oracle); cf. Plutarch, Life of Alexander 27
suggested_refs: The Temple of the Oracle at Aghurmi, Siwa Oasis
The 'Horns of Ammon' on later coin portraits of Alexander

segments.name: The Fall of the Great King

stops.name: Gaugamela, the eclipse and the broken center
stops.campa: Eleven nights before the battle the moon rises full and turns to blood over the Persian camp and goes dark; the Magi read it as ruin for the king of kings, and Alexander tells his own frightened men it foretells a Persian, not a Macedonian, eclipse. When Parmenion urges a night attack against Darius's far larger host, Alexander refuses outright: he will not steal a victory. At dawn he drives a wedge through the weakened Persian center exactly where he chose to strike; Darius flees the field a second time, and the empire of Cyrus and Darius the Great effectively ends before noon.
stops.quote: I will not steal my victory.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 31 (Perrin), to Parmenio on the eve of the battle; Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.10 reports the same refusal indirectly
suggested_refs: The Alexander Mosaic (again depicting Darius's flight, conflating Issus and Gaugamela in later memory)

stops.name: Babylon, the gates opened to the conqueror
stops.campa: Babylon, greatest city the army has seen, sends out its priests and nobles with garlands, gifts, and open gates rather than face a siege; the Persian satrap Mazaeus himself surrenders the citadel. Alexander enters in state along the processional way to Esagila, sacrifices to Bel-Marduk as the Chaldean priests direct, and orders the temple, left to ruin under Xerxes, rebuilt at his own expense. He confirms Mazaeus in his satrapy, the first Persian so honored, and lets his weary men rest a month in a city whose luxury, the Macedonian officers mutter, may prove more dangerous than any Persian army.
suggested_refs: The Ishtar Gate and processional way of Babylon
The temple of Esagila, ordered rebuilt by Alexander

stops.name: Susa, the treasure of the Achaemenids
stops.campa: Susa yields without a blow and with it the accumulated treasury of the House of Cyrus and Darius: fifty thousand talents of gold and silver bullion, dyed Hermione purple worth its own weight untouched for a hundred and eighty years, and the royal chair itself, on which Alexander sits, his feet too short for the Persian footstool the servants have brought, so that a page slides a table under them instead. Among the spoil Alexander finds the bronze statues of the tyrannicides Harmodius and Aristogeiton, carried off by Xerxes from Athens a century and a half before, and sends them home.
suggested_refs: The Apadana of Susa, throne hall of the Achaemenids
The statues of Harmodius and Aristogeiton, restored to Athens

stops.name: Persepolis, the palace burned
stops.campa: Ceremonial capital of the kings, Persepolis surrenders its treasury of one hundred and twenty thousand talents and is given over to four months of plunder, the harshest sack of the whole campaign, Alexander tells his men, in payment for Xerxes's burning of Athens a century and a half before. At a night's banquet the Athenian courtesan Thais rises, torch in hand, and calls on the company to finish what Xerxes began and burn the palace of Xerxes down; Alexander, they say, is the first to fling his own torch onto the cedar roof-beams, and the fire spreads from hall to hall until dawn.
suggested_refs: The blackened, fire-scarred columns of the Apadana at Persepolis, still visible today

stops.name: The road to Hecatompylos, the death of the Great King
stops.campa: Fleeing east from his own collapsing empire, Darius is seized by his kinsman Bessus and the satrap Nabarzanes, bound in golden fetters, and carried in a covered ox-cart as Alexander's cavalry closes the distance in a killing forced march. Overtaken at last, the conspirators stab Darius and abandon him and flee; a Macedonian soldier finds the last king of Persia dying alone in the wagon. Alexander comes too late to speak with him, but covers the body with his own cloak and sends it on to Persepolis for burial among the tombs of his royal predecessors, a king honoring a king.
suggested_refs: The Naqsh-e Rustam royal tombs near Persepolis, resting place of the Achaemenid kings

segments.name: To the Ends of the Earth: Bactria and Sogdia

stops.name: Ecbatana, the punishment of the regicide
stops.campa: Bessus has proclaimed himself Great King under the name Artaxerxes, but his own officers, seeing Alexander's pursuit gaining, seize him and hand him over naked and bound beside the road. Alexander orders him tried before an assembly of Persians and Medes for the murder of his own lord Darius, and condemns him to the old Persian penalty for regicide: nose and ears sliced away, and death by impalement or crucifixion on the very spot, some say, where Darius breathed his last. It is the harshest sentence Alexander passes on any man, and he passes it as a Persian king, not a Greek one.
suggested_refs: The Behistun inscription, recording Darius I's identical punishment of the usurper Phraortes, precedent for Bessus's sentence

stops.name: Maracanda, the death of Cleitus
stops.campa: At a drunken banquet in Sogdian Maracanda, flatterers belittle Philip's victories to exalt Alexander's own, and Cleitus, the very man who saved his life at the Granicus, rises in fury to defend the old king's memory and to mock the Persian dress and the claims of divine sonship his king has begun to entertain. Alexander lunges for a weapon; his own guards disarm and hustle Cleitus from the hall, but the man forces his way back in to finish his taunts, and Alexander seizes a sentry's spear and runs him through. He weeps over the body for three days and will not eat.
suggested_refs: The site of ancient Maracanda beneath modern Samarkand's Afrasiyab mound

stops.name: The far Jaxartes, the Land of Darkness and the Water of Life
stops.campa: At Alexandria Eschate, the farthest city he will found, the edge of the mapped world gives way, in the fuller telling, to a country the sun does not reach. Alexander enters it with his cook Andreas, called in the Persian retelling by the name of the mysterious guide al-Khidr, seeking the spring that grants unending life. Andreas, sent to wash a dried and salted fish in a fountain along the way, watches it stir and swim off whole; he drinks there himself before he understands what water this is, and gains what his king, arriving a step behind him, does not.
suggested_refs: Persian manuscript illuminations of 'Alexander and Khidr enter the Land of Darkness' (e.g. the Book of Felicity)
sources: Alexander Romance, Pseudo-Callisthenes / Syriac and Persian recensions
Qur'an 18:60-82 (the parallel Khidr narrative, Surat al-Kahf)

stops.name: The Caucasus Gate against Gog and Magog
stops.campa: Between two mountains at the world's northern hinge, the two-horned king finds a people who beg him for a wall against the savage nations of Gog and Magog, who ravage the land and devour its people. He commands iron brought and melted with copper poured over it until the pass itself is sealed in an unbreakable barrier, closing the raiders in behind the mountains until the appointed day. He tells them plainly that it is by his Lord's mercy alone this labor is finished, and that when the true promise comes the wall itself will be leveled to dust as foretold.
stops.quote: This is a mercy from my Lord: but when the promise of my Lord comes to pass, He will make it into dust; and the promise of my Lord is ever true.
suggested_refs: The Caspian Gates / Darband Wall at Derbent, long identified with the Gate of Alexander
Surat al-Kahf 18:83-98, the Dhul-Qarnayn passage
sources: Alexander Romance, Gog and Magog episode

stops.name: The Sogdian Rock, men with wings
stops.campa: A Sogdian stronghold on a sheer, snow-slicked cliff, provisioned for years and holding the family of the noble Oxyartes, answers Alexander's demand to surrender by laughing that he would need soldiers with wings to take it. Three hundred men who have learned rock-climbing on earlier sieges scale the face by night on tent-pegs and flaxen ropes, losing thirty of their number to the fall; at dawn Alexander's herald shouts up to the garrison that the winged men have indeed been found, and points to the armed Macedonians standing along the summit above their heads. The rock surrenders without another blow struck.
stops.quote: The winged men have been found, and the summits of the mountain are in their possession.
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 4.19 (the message Alexander orders his herald to shout up to the garrison); Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 7.11
suggested_refs: The Sogdian Rock (Koh-i-Nor), near modern Baysun, Uzbekistan

stops.name: Bactra, the marriage of Roxana
stops.campa: Among the captives taken at the Sogdian Rock is Oxyartes's daughter Roxana, said by every man in the army who sees her dancing at the victory feast to be the loveliest woman in Asia after the wife of Darius. Alexander, who has resisted the beds of every conquered queen, falls for this one at first sight and will have her as a wife and not a captive, over the grumbling of Macedonians who wanted a Macedonian queen. The marriage is sealed in the Macedonian fashion, bread cut with a sword and shared; it binds the Bactrian and Sogdian nobility to his throne as no conquest could.
suggested_refs: Ancient Bactra (Balkh), the traditional site of Alexander's wedding to Roxana

segments.name: India: to the Hyphasis and Back

stops.name: Taxila, the riddles of the naked philosophers
stops.campa: King Taxiles submits without a fight and Alexander enters Taxila, greatest city between the Indus and the Hydaspes, where he meets a company of ascetics the Greeks call gymnosophists, naked philosophers who own nothing and fear nothing, not even the king. Curious and half in earnest, Alexander sets them a contest of riddles, declaring that whoever answers worst each round will be put to death first and the rest in order after; asked whether the living or the dead are more numerous, the eldest answers that the dead are not, since they no longer exist, and the sages are sent home with gifts instead.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Taxila (Sirkap), UNESCO World Heritage Site

stops.name: Hydaspes, the king who asked to be treated as a king
stops.campa: Porus, ruler of the lands beyond the Hydaspes, draws up eighty-five war elephants and a great army on the swollen river's far bank; Alexander crosses upstream by night in a thunderstorm, feints, and defeats him in the hardest battle of the whole campaign. Wounded, still mounted, and defeated, Porus is brought before Alexander, who asks how he wishes to be treated. He answers as a king, and nothing less; moved, Alexander restores his kingdom to him whole and adds new provinces besides, keeping in Porus, for the rest of his own life, one of the most loyal of all his subject-allies.
stops.quote: For my own sake, Porus, thou shalt be thus treated; but for thy own sake do thou demand what is pleasing to thee!
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 5.19 (Chinnock), Alexander's answer after Porus asks to be treated in a kingly way; cf. Plutarch, Life of Alexander 60
suggested_refs: The Hydaspes (Jhelum) river, site of Alexander's last great pitched battle

stops.name: The death of Bucephalus and the founding of two cities
stops.campa: Bucephalus, ridden by Alexander since the boy tamed him at twelve years old, dies here on the Hydaspes, some say of wounds taken in the battle against Porus, some say simply of great age, having carried his king across three continents for thirty years. Alexander's grief is as public as any he shows in the whole campaign; he gives the horse full funeral honors and founds a city on the spot and names it Bucephala in his memory, raising a second city, Nicaea, opposite it on the river to commemorate the victory that this same horse had carried him to.
suggested_refs: Bucephala and Nicaea, the twin cities Alexander founded on the Hydaspes

stops.name: The Trees of the Sun and Moon foretell his death
stops.campa: Advancing still further into India, Alexander is led by his Indian guides to a temple grove where two great trees stand, one sacred to the Sun and male, one sacred to the Moon and female, both able to speak with a human voice at dawn and at dusk. Alexander asks whether he will return home to see his mother and to rule the whole world; the Tree of the Sun answers that he will be lord of all the earth, but the Tree of the Moon tells him, weeping, that he will die by poison in Babylon within the year, and will not name the hand.
suggested_refs: The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle, the earliest source for the Trees of the Sun and Moon
sources: Alexander Romance, Pseudo-Callisthenes recension (Trees of the Sun and Moon episode)
The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle

stops.name: The ascent by griffins
stops.campa: Not content to have mastered the earth, Alexander wishes to see it whole from above as the gods do. He has two griffins of the eastern mountains caught and starved, yokes them to a wicker cage, and dangles meat on spears just beyond their reach so that they beat upward endlessly, straining after the bait, lifting the king higher into the sky than any mortal has climbed. A winged shape meets him among the clouds and warns him that he has not yet secured the whole earth below him and has no business exploring the heaven above it; he turns the cage back down.
suggested_refs: Medieval reliefs and mosaics of the 'Flight of Alexander' (e.g. Otranto Cathedral, San Marco Venice)
sources: Alexander Romance, Pseudo-Callisthenes recension gamma (the griffin-flight episode)
The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle

stops.name: Hyphasis, the altars of the turning back
stops.campa: At the river Hyphasis, the eastern edge of everything the Macedonians have been told about India, the army stops walking. Years of marches, wounds, monsoon rain, and rumor of vast kingdoms and thousands more elephants waiting beyond the river break the soldiers' will at last; Coenus rises to speak for all of them, and is met by Alexander with silence rather than fury. For two days the king sulks alone in his tent; on the third he yields, and has twelve altars raised on the riverbank, tall as towers, to mark the farthest limit the Macedonian arms will ever reach going east.
stops.quote: I, for my part, think that to a brave man there is no end to labours except the labours themselves, provided they lead to glorious achievements.
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 5.26 (Chinnock), Alexander's speech to the army at the Hyphasis
suggested_refs: The twelve altars of the Hyphasis, described by Arrian and Diodorus, site now lost

stops.name: The Mallian town, the arrow in the breast
stops.campa: Sailing and marching down the Indus against the last unsubdued peoples, Alexander storms a Mallian citadel so impatiently that he scales the wall himself with only three companions before the ladders behind him break. Trapped alone inside with the enemy closing, he leaps down among them rather than wait; an arrow punches through his breastplate into his chest so deep that air is heard hissing from the wound with his blood, and he very nearly dies before his men break in, tear down the wall itself, and carry his unconscious body back to the camp on his own shield.
suggested_refs: The sacred shield of Troy, held over Alexander's body by Peucestas during the Mallian wound

stops.name: The Gedrosian desert, the helmet poured on the sand
stops.campa: Choosing the hardest road home to punish the desert as it once punished a Persian army, Alexander leads his men across the sands of Gedrosia, where heat, thirst, and flash floods kill more of the army than any battle of the whole campaign. Scouts find a trickle of water in a hollow and bring it to him cupped in a helmet; with every man around him as parched as himself, Alexander thanks them and pours it out on the ground untasted rather than drink alone. The army, watching, is said to have found in that single gesture strength enough to keep marching.
suggested_refs: Tom Lovell's 'Alexander the Great Refuses Water in the Desert' (1968), depicting this episode

stops.name: Pasargadae, the tomb of Cyrus defiled and restored
stops.campa: Alexander comes again to the plain stone tomb of Cyrus the Great, whose epitaph he had once read and wept to think that so small a house of earth was all that remained of so vast an empire. This time he finds the tomb broken open, the golden couch stripped, the coffin lid gone and the king's bones scattered by robbers. Grieved past the loss of any treasure, he has the Magi who guarded it questioned under torture; when none will confess, he lets them go unpunished, and orders his officer Aristobulus to gather Cyrus's bones, mend the couch, and seal the tomb again in stone.
suggested_refs: The Tomb of Cyrus the Great at Pasargadae (UNESCO World Heritage), restored on Alexander's order
The tomb-epitaph read here by Alexander: 'O man, I am Cyrus... do not begrudge me this little earth' (shared with cyrus.journey.json)

stops.name: Susa, the marriage of the two crowns
stops.campa: In a vast pavilion of purple and gold at Susa, Alexander celebrates in a single ceremony some eighty marriages between his Macedonian officers and daughters of the Persian nobility, sealing the fusion of conqueror and conquered he has pursued since the Roxana wedding. He himself takes Stateira, eldest daughter of Darius, and Parysatis, daughter of a former Great King, as wives beside Roxana; ten thousand common soldiers who have taken Asian wives on campaign receive wedding gifts from the royal treasury as well. It is the high tide of his dream of one people; within a year his officers will quietly set the Persian brides aside.
suggested_refs: The Susa weddings, described by Arrian and Chares of Mytilene, master of ceremonies
sources: Chares of Mytilene, fragment on the Susa weddings

stops.name: Opis, the mutiny and the banquet of nations
stops.campa: When Alexander announces the discharge of his aged Macedonian veterans and their replacement by trained Persian troops, the army mutinies at once, mocking his claimed divine father and telling him to conquer on with Ammon's help alone. He leaps down among them, has the ringleaders seized and executed on the spot, then shuts himself away two days. When the men gather weeping at his door, ashamed, he receives them back, embraces them, and holds a vast reconciling banquet where Macedonians and Persians drink from the same bowl, and he prays aloud for harmony between the two peoples, calling the whole assembly, at last, his kinsmen.
stops.quote: But all of you without exception I consider my kinsmen, and so from this time I shall call you.
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 7.11 (Chinnock), the reconciliation at Opis
suggested_refs: Arrian's full text of the Opis mutiny and reconciliation, Anabasis Book 7

stops.name: Ecbatana, the death of Hephaestion
stops.campa: Hephaestion, Alexander's companion since boyhood, whom he has called the friend dearer to him than any other and all but named his second self, falls ill of fever at Ecbatana and dies within the week, before Alexander can be brought from the games he is watching. Alexander flings himself on the body and will not be moved for a day, has his hair cut short in Homeric mourning, and orders a shrine to Asclepius torn down for failing to save him. A funeral pyre of unheard-of size and cost is commissioned for Babylon, and Hephaestion is decreed to be worshipped thereafter as a hero of the gods.
suggested_refs: The planned 60-meter funeral pyre for Hephaestion at Babylon, costing 10,000 talents

segments.name: Babylon and the Death of the King

stops.name: Babylon, the omens gather
stops.campa: Returning to Babylon to make it the capital of his whole empire, Alexander is met on the road by Chaldean priests who warn him, in the name of their god Bel, not to enter the city facing west, toward the setting sun. He tries to enter from the east instead, but the marshes force him back onto the forbidden road regardless. Once inside, the omens multiply: a tame donkey kills the finest lion in his menagerie with a single kick; an unknown man is found sitting calmly on the royal throne in royal robes, and can give no account of how he came there.
suggested_refs: The Babylonian Astronomical Diaries, contemporary cuneiform record of the last months of Alexander's reign

stops.name: Babylon, the death of Alexander
stops.campa: After a banquet and a night of heavy drinking in Nearchus's honor, Alexander is seized by fever that will not break; for eleven days it climbs, until he can no longer speak and his officers, filing past his bed one last time, see only his eyes move to follow them. Asked to whom he leaves his kingdom, he is said to answer with his last clear word, before the fever takes his voice for good. He dies not yet thirty-three years old, having conquered from Greece to India, and having, by his own reckoning, still more world left ungoverned than any man before or since.
stops.quote_source: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.117; Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 7.26; Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 10.5
suggested_refs: The Babylonian Astronomical Diary recording Alexander's death, 11th of Aiaru (10 June 323 BC)

stops.name: Alexandria, the tomb of the god-king
stops.campa: The funeral cortege built to carry Alexander's embalmed body back to be buried among the kings of Macedon at Aegae never reaches home: Ptolemy, his companion since boyhood and now satrap of Egypt, intercepts the golden funeral carriage in Syria and diverts it south to the city Alexander marked out himself in barley meal. He is laid first at Memphis, in the ancient capital he had once been crowned pharaoh, and afterward moved to a tomb in Alexandria itself, where for centuries emperors and philosophers will come to look upon his embalmed face, in the city that outlived every empire he conquered.
suggested_refs: The lost Soma, Alexander's mausoleum at Alexandria, visited by Julius Caesar, Augustus, and Caracalla in antiquity
